_comment: Hand-written editorial layer for the Higher/Lower game. Keys are
`<metric>-<iso3>-<iso3>` with the two country codes sorted alphabetically, so
a key survives a data refresh even when the underlying year changes.
`winner` is a guard, not data: generate-questions.js refuses to ship a
question whose winner no longer matches, because the insight line was written
about a specific direction and would otherwise silently become false.
Insight rule of thumb: if the sentence would still be true and interesting to
someone who never sees the numbers, it works. Restating the values does not.

solar-DEU-FRA.insight: Cloudy Germany out-solars sunny France by almost 3x. Sunlight was never the constraint; installed panels are.

solar-GBR-ITA.insight: Italy produces well over twice Britain's solar power. Rooftop subsidies in the 2010s, not latitude, opened the gap.

solar-ESP-NLD.insight: Spain wins on raw output, but the Netherlands is one of Europe's cloudiest countries and lands in the same league. Panel count beats sunshine hours.

solar-CHL-GBR.insight: Chile's Atacama desert is the sunniest place on earth and most of its solar fleet sits there. Britain gets a comparable total from a country with a fraction of the sunlight.

solar-NLD-PAK.insight: Pakistan's solar output has grown roughly nine-fold in five years and now passes the Netherlands. Cheap imported panels plus an unreliable grid pushed households and factories to generate their own power.

solar-IND-JPN.insight: India passed Japan on solar roughly a decade after starting seriously. Solar is now the cheapest new power in most of the world, so it scales fastest where demand is still growing.

solar-DEU-ESP.insight: Germany still out-produces Spain on solar with roughly half the sunshine. It started twenty years earlier and never stopped installing.

wind-FRA-GBR.insight: Britain built the world's largest offshore wind fleet while France bet on nuclear. Both are low-carbon strategies; they just look nothing alike.

wind-BRA-DEU.insight: Germany still leads on total output, but Brazil's northeastern trade winds are among the steadiest on earth, so each Brazilian turbine earns far more than a German one.

wind-BRA-IND.insight: Brazil out-produces India on wind with a fifth of the population. Its northeastern coast has unusually constant trade winds, which lifts output per turbine dramatically.

wind-CAN-ESP.insight: Spain has been a wind pioneer since the 1990s. Canada has far more windy land and far fewer people on it - geography alone doesn't build turbines.

wind-AUS-SWE.insight: Sweden generates more wind power than Australia with about a third of the population. Australia's renewable build leaned into rooftop solar instead, where it leads the world.

wind-DNK-TUR.insight: Denmark invented the modern wind industry and gets a larger share of its power from wind than any country on earth. It is also small, so its total output is easily beaten.

nuclear_pct-BEL-SVK.insight: Slovakia draws two thirds of its electricity from nuclear, among the highest shares in the world. Belgium has been legislating a nuclear phase-out since 2003 and postponing it ever since.

nuclear_pct-SWE-UKR.insight: Even through a full-scale invasion, Ukraine ran most of its grid on nuclear. Reactors are hard to build, and equally hard to replace once you depend on them.

nuclear_pct-KOR-USA.insight: The US operates far more reactors than South Korea, but its grid is so much bigger that nuclear's share comes out smaller. Absolute size and share routinely tell opposite stories.

nuclear_pct-ESP-GBR.insight: Britain opened the world's first commercial nuclear plant in 1956, and most of that fleet has since retired. Spain's newer reactors now carry the bigger share.

nuclear_pct-CZE-SWE.insight: Sweden closed four reactors in the 2010s and has since reversed course politically. Czechia never wavered, and now leans on nuclear harder than Sweden does.

nuclear_pct-FIN-KOR.insight: Finland's Olkiluoto 3 took some seventeen years to build, but a single reactor was enough to visibly shift a small country's entire electricity mix.

coal_pct-CHN-IND.insight: China burns far more coal than India in absolute terms, yet has also built more wind, solar and hydro than anyone. India's grid is the more coal-dependent of the two.

coal_pct-AUS-DEU.insight: Germany takes the criticism for coal; Australia quietly runs on twice as much of it, and exports more of it than almost any country on earth.

coal_pct-AUS-POL.insight: Poland's grid was built on domestic hard coal and lignite, and mining employment has made retiring it politically expensive. Australia is on a similar path, a few years further along.

coal_pct-KOR-TWN.insight: Taiwan has been phasing out nuclear while electricity demand from chip fabrication climbs. Coal and gas filled the gap. South Korea kept its reactors.

coal_pct-DEU-RUS.insight: Russia is a fossil fuel superpower that burns gas rather than coal at home - it has more gas than it can profitably sell. Germany still leans on lignite it can dig up domestically.

coal_pct-IND-KAZ.insight: Both grids run on domestic coal. India's is the more dependent, and it is also the fastest-growing large electricity market in the world.

clean_pct-ESP-GBR.insight: Britain's coal-to-wind switch is one of the fastest grid decarbonisations ever recorded. Spain got further still, using solar and hydro Britain simply doesn't have.

clean_pct-AUT-CHE.insight: Switzerland runs on Alpine hydro plus nuclear and is effectively fossil-free. Austria has the same mountains but no reactors, so gas fills its winter gaps.

clean_pct-CAN-KEN.insight: Kenya runs on Rift Valley geothermal plus hydro and wind, giving it one of the cleanest grids on earth. Clean electricity is not a rich-country privilege.

clean_pct-BEL-SVK.insight: Both lean on nuclear, but Slovakia leans harder and adds Danube hydro on top. Belgium's long-running phase-out politics keep pulling its share down.

clean_pct-GRC-USA.insight: Greece went from lignite-dominated to majority-clean in about fifteen years. The US has more clean generation than any country except China, and still a dirtier average.

clean_pct-BRA-CAN.insight: Both grids were built on big hydro. Brazil added wind and solar on top; Canada's remaining fossil generation is concentrated in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

independence-DEU-FRA.insight: France's reactors sit on French soil, but France mines no uranium at all - every fuel rod is imported. Independence is about where the fuel comes from, not where the plant stands.

independence-ITA-JPN.insight: Japan imports almost all its fossil fuel and shut most of its reactors after Fukushima, leaving it among the most import-exposed developed economies.

independence-NGA-POL.insight: Nigeria runs its grid on its own gas and hydro, so on paper it imports nothing. This score measures import exposure, not reliability - Nigerian supply still fails constantly.

independence-DEU-DNK.insight: Denmark's wind fleet needs no fuel deliveries, which is exactly what this score rewards. Germany still buys gas and hard coal from abroad.

independence-AUT-IND.insight: Austrian Alpine hydro needs no fuel at all. India burns a great deal of coal but digs most of it up itself, which is why it scores better here than its emissions would suggest.

generation_per_capita-CAN-USA.insight: Canada generates more electricity per person than the US: cold winters, heavy industry, and hydro cheap enough to make electric heating the rational choice.

generation_per_capita-DEU-SWE.insight: Sweden generates nearly three times Germany's electricity per person. Abundant hydro and nuclear made power cheap enough to electrify heating and heavy industry.

generation_per_capita-CHE-KWT.insight: Kuwait's air conditioning and seawater desalination run on heavily subsidised domestic gas. Cheap energy always gets used, whatever the climate demands.

generation_per_capita-NOR-USA.insight: Norway generates more than twice as much electricity per person as the US. Near-free hydro attracted aluminium smelters and made electrifying everything else the default.

generation_per_capita-CHN-ESP.insight: China now generates more electricity per person than Spain. No single number captures how far its industrialisation has run more clearly than this one.

generation_per_capita-KOR-SGP.insight: Both are dense, rich and urban. South Korea's steel, shipbuilding and semiconductor plants push it above Singapore's services-and-trade economy.

generation_per_capita-JPN-NLD.insight: Japan out-generates the Netherlands per person despite a decade of hard-won post-Fukushima efficiency gains. Industrial structure sets the floor.

total_generation-JPN-RUS.insight: Russia out-generates Japan. Cheap domestic gas and an energy-intensive heavy industry base make electricity worth using in ways it simply isn't in Japan.

total_generation-GBR-TUR.insight: Turkey overtook Britain and keeps pulling away. British electricity demand has been flat or falling since 2005 as industry shrank and efficiency improved.

total_generation-FRA-IRN.insight: France's nuclear fleet gives it one of Europe's largest grids and makes it a net exporter to its neighbours in most years.

total_generation-BRA-JPN.insight: Japan generates more electricity from 125 million people than Brazil does from 215 million. Wealth and industry drive electricity use far harder than headcount.

total_generation-MYS-POL.insight: Malaysia out-generates Poland from a similar population. Southeast Asian electricity demand is growing at rates Europe last saw in the 1960s.

total_generation-POL-THA.insight: Thailand out-generates Poland. The centre of gravity in global electricity has moved decisively to Asia, and it is still moving.

emissions-DEU-JPN.insight: Japan's power sector emits roughly triple Germany's, largely because the reactors idled after Fukushima were backfilled with coal and gas.

emissions-AUS-CAN.insight: Australia and Canada have similar populations and similar wealth. Canada's grid is hydro and nuclear, Australia's is still substantially coal - same conditions, opposite outcome.

emissions-VNM-ZAF.insight: South Africa's grid is almost entirely coal, run by a single struggling utility. Vietnam is growing fast but has added serious solar alongside its coal.

emissions-BRA-POL.insight: Poland has roughly a fifth of Brazil's population and higher power sector emissions. Brazil's hydro-heavy grid is the entire difference.

emissions-FRA-SGP.insight: France's whole grid, serving 68 million people, emits less carbon than Singapore's, serving under 6 million. Nuclear and hydro are the reason.

wind-ESP-FRA.insight: Spain built wind farms through the 1990s while France was finishing its nuclear fleet. A country that already has cheap low-carbon power has less reason to add more.

wind-DEU-IND.insight: Germany still out-produces India on wind despite roughly a seventeenth of the population. India's build-out is faster, but it started from almost nothing two decades later.

coal_pct-DEU-USA.insight: American coal was displaced by its own shale gas rather than by climate policy - cheaper fuel simply won. Germany kept burning domestic lignite it can dig up itself.

coal_pct-AUS-KAZ.insight: Kazakhstan sits on enormous coal reserves and burns them at home while exporting its oil and uranium. Selling the valuable fuel and burning the cheap one is a common pattern.

independence-FRA-IRL.insight: Ireland imports nearly all its gas, but the wind it runs on needs no supplier at all. France's reactors are domestic and every gram of their uranium is not.

independence-GRC-ROU.insight: Romania is the rare EU country with meaningful domestic gas and oil, plus Carpathian hydro and a reactor. Greece buys almost all of its fuel from abroad.

generation_per_capita-CHN-DEU.insight: China now generates more electricity per person than Germany. The country that was the world's cheap factory has quietly passed the economy it was making things for.

total_generation-DEU-KOR.insight: South Korea out-generates Germany from a population barely half the size. Semiconductors, steel and shipbuilding are extraordinarily electricity-hungry industries.

total_generation-EGY-VNM.insight: Vietnam's grid has roughly tripled this century as manufacturing moved in from China. Electricity demand is the clearest early signal of an industrialising economy.

emissions-CAN-DEU.insight: Germany's power sector still out-emits Canada's despite a far larger renewable fleet, because what renewables replaced was nuclear rather than lignite.

emissions-CZE-FRA.insight: Czechia has around a seventh of France's population and a dirtier grid in absolute terms. Coal at a small scale beats nuclear at a large one, for emissions.

clean_pct-KGZ-URY.insight: Uruguay rebuilt its grid in about a decade: an auction programme begun in 2009 offered twenty-year fixed prices, and wind went from nothing to its single largest source. Kyrgyzstan's score comes from Soviet-era hydro it has simply kept running - the same clean result, arrived at by standing still.

clean_pct-ECU-LUX.insight: Luxembourg imports more than three quarters of the electricity it uses, so its clean score describes only the sliver it generates itself, which is now almost all wind, solar and biomass. Ecuador's number covers a grid that actually meets its own demand, nearly all of it hydro.

solar-HUN-PRT.insight: Hungary out-produces sunnier Portugal on solar, and a large share of it sits on houses: a net-metering scheme made domestic panels pay back fast enough that rooftops became a third of national capacity. Latitude set the ceiling; the tariff decided who got near it.

wind-NZL-URY.insight: These two generate almost the same amount of wind power, and it means completely different things - roughly a tenth of New Zealand's hydro-dominated grid, and about forty per cent of Uruguay's. The same turbines can be a rounding error or the backbone.

total_generation-NGA-PRT.insight: Portugal generates more electricity than Nigeria, from a country with a twentieth of the people. Nigeria's problem is not fuel or even power stations: its transmission network can carry only about half the capacity that is already built, so much of it never reaches anyone.

generation_per_capita-BLR-EST.insight: Belarus had no nuclear power at all in 2020; the Russian-built Astravets plant now supplies more than a third of its electricity and pushed output to a record. Estonia moved the other way, generation more than halving as it wound down the oil shale that once ran the country.

coal_pct-BGR-LKA.insight: Sri Lanka's coal is essentially one power station - Lakvijaya, opened in 2011 and finished in 2014 - which alone carries roughly a quarter of the grid. Bulgaria has spent twenty years going the other way, its coal share falling as nuclear held steady and solar arrived.

emissions-BGR-DOM.insight: The Dominican Republic emits more from electricity than Bulgaria while generating substantially less of it. Three quarters of what it burns is coal, gas or oil; most of Bulgaria's power comes from a nuclear plant and its rivers.

clean_pct-LKA-MMR.insight: Both grids were built on hydro and both have been diluted by fossil fuel since. Sri Lanka has started clawing it back with solar, which now supplies about a sixth of its power; in Myanmar, gas has grown as fast as the dams have.

independence-ARG-ECU.insight: Ecuador scores higher for the simple reason that water needs no fuel supply chain. Argentina produces most of the gas it burns, which is genuinely unusual and valuable - but a grid that runs on fuel still depends on continuing to pull it out of the ground.

generation_per_capita-CRI-MNG.insight: Mongolia uses more electricity per person than Costa Rica and burns coal for nearly all of it, because mining alone takes around forty per cent of national demand. Costa Rica's grid is effectively fully renewable, but serves an economy that asks less of it.

coal_pct-BGD-THA.insight: Bangladesh had almost no coal power a decade ago and now leans on it more heavily than Thailand does. Its domestic gas fields have been declining faster than imported LNG could cover, and a run of new coal plants from 2020 onward filled the gap.

generation_per_capita-MDA-MNG.insight: Mongolia's higher figure is industrial rather than domestic: mining alone accounts for around forty per cent of national demand, and coal supplies nearly all of it. Moldova runs on gas for close to nine tenths of its power and asks less of the grid overall.

generation_per_capita-COL-ECU.insight: Two Andean grids built on the same mountain rivers, and Ecuador gets more electricity per person out of them. Both are unusually exposed to weather: when the reservoirs drop, so does the national power supply.

generation_per_capita-MEX-MKD.insight: North Macedonia has fewer people than many single cities and still generates more electricity per person than Mexico. Small grids often do - one large plant or industrial site moves the per-person figure in a way nothing can across 130 million people.

generation_per_capita-AZE-LUX.insight: This flatters neither country. Luxembourg imports more than three quarters of the electricity it uses, so the figure measures only what it bothers to make itself; Azerbaijan makes nearly all of its own, and burns gas for close to nine tenths of it.

total_generation-BLR-HUN.insight: Both lean on a single reactor site for a large share of their power - Hungary on Paks, Belarus on Astravets, which only opened in 2020. The difference is what fills the rest: Hungary has been adding solar at pace, while Belarus still burns gas for over half.

total_generation-BLR-OMN.insight: Oman generates more electricity than Belarus with barely half the population. Almost all of it is gas, and much of it goes on cooling buildings and making fresh water - two things a Gulf summer demands relentlessly and a Belarusian one does not.

total_generation-MAR-OMN.insight: Oman generates more electricity than Morocco from about a seventh of the people. Per person the gap is enormous: Morocco produces roughly a tenth of what Oman does, which is less a fact about power stations than about how differently the two countries live.

total_generation-BGD-PHL.insight: The Philippines generates more electricity than Bangladesh from a third fewer people. Both depend heavily on imported fuel, and both have spent the last decade adding coal rather than replacing it.

clean_pct-BOL-NGA.insight: These two grids are near-twins in shape despite having nothing else in common: roughly two thirds gas, most of the rest hydro. Both found gas at home and built around it, which is the most common way a country ends up neither clean nor dirty.

clean_pct-GEO-LUX.insight: Georgia's four fifths comes from rivers powering a grid that nearly meets its own demand. Luxembourg's higher score covers only the fifth of its electricity it actually generates - the rest arrives over the border carrying whatever its neighbours happened to burn.

clean_pct-ARG-MMR.insight: Myanmar edges ahead on a near-even split between its dams and its gas fields. Argentina's mix is broader - gas, hydro, wind and a nuclear programme running since the 1970s - but gas still carries more than half of it.

clean_pct-CYP-MAR.insight: Cyprus ran on oil and nothing else for most of this century, and is now roughly a quarter clean on solar alone. An island with no cable to anywhere pays for every barrel it lands; Morocco has more sun and less pressure, and imported coal still carries most of its grid.

clean_pct-EST-MMR.insight: Estonia ran on oil shale, among the dirtiest fuels in Europe, for the whole of the last century - and has cut it from nearly all its electricity to under half in about fifteen years. Myanmar has drifted the other way, its gas growing as fast as its dams.

clean_pct-LUX-SVN.insight: Slovenia's score rests on one reactor and its rivers, though half of Krsko's output belongs to Croatia under a 50-50 agreement - the plant sits on Slovenia's books while the electricity leaves. Luxembourg's higher figure covers only the fifth of its supply it makes at all.

clean_pct-MAR-SRB.insight: Two coal grids at almost the same clean share, reached from opposite directions. Serbia's quarter is hydro on the Danube and its tributaries, built decades ago; Morocco's is wind and solar built in the last fifteen years, on top of coal it kept adding at the same time.

emissions-BOL-ECU.insight: Bolivia emits more from a grid barely a third the size of Ecuador's. Ecuador's power is mostly falling water and Bolivia's is mostly burning gas - proof that how much a country generates says very little about what it emits.

emissions-BOL-LKA.insight: Bolivia emits more than Sri Lanka while generating less electricity. Gas is the cleaner fuel per unit burned, but Bolivia burns it for two thirds of its power, while more than half of Sri Lanka's comes from water and sun.

emissions-MMR-PRI.insight: Puerto Rico emits more from electricity than Myanmar, with a population seventeen times smaller. Almost half its power still comes from oil, a fuel most grids abandoned decades ago - an island that ships in every drop has no cheap clean option waiting on the shelf.

coal_pct-KGZ-SVN.insight: Slovenia is on its way out of coal: a third of the grid at the turn of the century, a seventh now, with nuclear and hydro carrying the load. Kyrgyzstan is heading the other way, burning more coal each year as demand outgrows what its dams can deliver.

coal_pct-MMR-TJK.insight: Neither burns much coal, and for the same reason - both grids were built on rivers. Tajikistan is the extreme case at around ninety-five per cent hydro, which leaves it exporting power in summer when the rivers are high and short of it every winter.

wind-LTU-THA.insight: Lithuania generates more wind power than Thailand from a country twenty-five times smaller. It had little choice: closing the Ignalina nuclear plant in 2009, a condition of joining the EU, removed roughly eighty per cent of its electricity.

wind-NZL-THA.insight: New Zealand out-produces Thailand on wind with a fourteenth of the population, though wind is still a junior partner at home behind hydro and geothermal. Thailand's constraint is not turbines but the wind itself, which is modest across most of the country.

wind-HRV-LTU.insight: Both built wind quickly, for different reasons. Croatia added it alongside long-standing hydro; Lithuania needed something to replace a nuclear plant it was required to close. Wind is now Lithuania's largest single source and Croatia's second.

solar-MAR-QAT.insight: Qatar generated no solar power at all until Al Kharsaah opened in 2022 - a country with abundant sun and even more abundant gas had no particular reason to hurry. Morocco, which imports every tonne of coal it burns, started far earlier.

solar-DOM-LKA.insight: Both are island grids paying import prices for fuel, which is the strongest argument for solar there is. Sri Lanka has taken it further, to roughly a sixth of its electricity against about a tenth in the Dominican Republic.

solar-LKA-OMN.insight: Sri Lanka produces more solar power than Oman, which has far more sun and far more money. Oman's first grid-scale solar plant only came online in 2021: when the gas is cheap and comes out of your own ground, there is little pressure to build anything else.

solar-LKA-QAT.insight: Sri Lanka took solar from almost nothing to roughly a sixth of its electricity in a handful of years. Qatar started later and from a far stronger position, and solar is still a rounding error on a grid that is otherwise entirely gas.
